intro: In 1882, a young teacher named Jigorō Kanō opened a small training room at a temple in Tokyo. Older fighting schools in Japan kept their lessons private. Kanō wanted lessons any school could share. He called his art judo.

Far away in England, boxers once fought with bare hands for prize money. In 1867, a page of twelve rules asked for gloves and timed rounds. In both places, a written code changed a rough fighting world into a sport with a start, an end and a referee.

In this unit, you will meet Kanō, his ranks and his ideas. You will compare judo's rules with the Queensberry Rules. By the end, you can explain how a rulebook helps a sport enter schools and the Olympics.
bigQuestion: How does writing rules down turn an old fighting practice into a school sport?

title: A School with a Rulebook

chapters.title: Kanō Writes Judo
chapters.bigQuestion: How did one teacher turn old fighting schools into a subject for a classroom?

story.title: A Desk Full of Old Scrolls
story.kicker: In Tokyo in the 1880s, a young teacher sorts through lessons from old schools.
paragraphs: Picture Tokyo in the early 1880s. Trains are new in Japan. Gas lamps light some streets. A young man named Jigorō Kanō sits at a low wooden desk. He has just finished university.

On the desk lie papers and rolled scrolls. They hold lessons from two old jujutsu schools where Kanō trained. Schools like these often kept their teaching in handwritten scrolls. Only trusted students could read them.
Kanō wants something different. He wants lessons that any student can learn in order. He wants a plan a school could follow, like a plan for reading or math.
In 1882, he opens a small training room at a Buddhist temple in Tokyo. He calls his school the Kodokan. He calls what he teaches judo. Over the next years he writes rules, ranks and aims for it.
Old schools were often secret and belonged to one family or teacher. Kanō's judo was meant to be shared. That choice helped judo travel from one temple room to schools around the world.
story.think: Why might a teacher want to write lessons down in an order that anyone can follow?

lessons.title: Many Old Schools
lessons.mainIdea: Before judo, Japan had many separate jujutsu schools, each with its own teacher, name and lessons.
reading: From 1603 to 1868, Japan was ruled by shoguns of the Tokugawa family. Historians call this the Edo period. The warrior class, the samurai, trained in many fighting arts. One group of arts was called *jujutsu*.

Jujutsu was not one school. There were many of them. Each school was called a *ryu*. A ryu had its own founder, its own name and its own lessons. Tenjin Shin'yo-ryu and Kito-ryu were two well-known ones.

Many ryu kept their teachings private. A teacher gave written scrolls only to trusted students. Some schools passed from father to son. So each school was a small world with its own habits and its own words.

words.d: a group of older Japanese arts of unarmed fighting, taught in many separate schools
a Japanese word for a school or line of teaching, passed from teacher to student

lessons.title: A New Japan in 1868
lessons.mainIdea: After 1868, Japan's government ended the samurai class and built public schools, and many jujutsu schools lost students.
reading: In 1868, Japan's shogun lost power. The emperor became the head of the country again. This change is called the *Meiji Restoration*. Meiji was the name of the emperor's era, from 1868 to 1912.

The new government changed Japan fast. It ended the special rank of the *samurai* in the 1870s. In 1876, a law stopped most people from wearing swords in public. Old warrior training seemed out of date to many people.
The government also built a school system for all children. A plan for it came out in 1872. Many jujutsu teachers lost their students in these years. Some schools closed for good.

lessons.title: Kanō Meets Jujutsu
lessons.mainIdea: Jigorō Kanō studied at Tokyo University and trained in two jujutsu schools before he made judo.
reading: Jigorō Kanō was born in 1860 in Mikage, near today's city of Kobe. In Japan, his name is written Kanō Jigorō, with the family name first. His family moved to Tokyo when he was a boy. He was a strong student in school.
Kanō studied at Tokyo University and finished in 1881. Stories about his youth say he was small and wanted to grow stronger. In the late 1870s, he began training in *Tenjin Shin'yo-ryu* jujutsu.

Later he trained in a second school, *Kito-ryu*, with a teacher named Iikubo Tsunetoshi. Each school taught different things. Kanō compared them. He kept parts he thought were useful and safe, and he dropped parts he thought were too dangerous.

words.d: an older jujutsu school where Kanō first trained

lessons.title: A Temple Room in 1882
lessons.mainIdea: In 1882, Kanō opened the Kodokan in a Buddhist temple in Tokyo, and it grew into judo's home school.
reading: In 1882, Kanō opened a small training room at Eisho-ji, a Buddhist temple in Tokyo. He was 21 years old. The room was tiny, and it was covered with straw mats. He had only a few students at first.
Kanō named his school the *Kodokan*. The name means a place for studying the way. A training room in Japanese arts is called a *dojo*. The Kodokan outgrew its first room and moved several times.
Today the Kodokan is a large building in the Bunkyo area of Tokyo. It keeps records of judo ranks and history. Many people call it the home of judo. It began in one temple room.

words.d: the judo school Kanō founded in Tokyo in 1882; its name means a place for studying the way
a training room in Japanese arts

lessons.title: Why a New Name
lessons.mainIdea: Kanō chose the name judo, the gentle way, to show his art was about study and growth, not only fighting.
reading: Jujutsu means the gentle art. Kanō changed the ending. He called his art *judo*, which means the gentle way. The word *do* means a way or a path in Japanese.

The ending do was used for other Japanese arts that aimed at learning and good habits. Kendo is the way of the sword. Sado is the way of tea. By choosing do, Kanō showed that judo was about building a person, not just winning.

The new name also helped in another way. In the 1880s, some people in Japan thought of jujutsu as rough and old-fashioned. A new name gave Kanō's school a fresh start. It set judo apart from the older ryu.

words.d: the gentle way; the art Jigorō Kanō founded at the Kodokan in 1882
a Japanese word meaning a way or a path

lessons.title: Three Goals in a Speech
lessons.mainIdea: In an 1889 speech, Kanō said judo trains the body, prepares for contests and builds the mind.
reading: Kanō was a teacher all his life. He taught at the Gakushuin, a school in Tokyo, and later led the Tokyo Higher Normal School. A *normal school* is a college that trains teachers. He led it for many years, until 1920.

In 1889, Kanō gave a *lecture*, or teaching speech, to a group of educators in Tokyo. He explained what judo was for. He named three goals. The first was physical education, for a healthy body. The second was contest. The third was training the mind.
These goals made judo sound like a school subject. That was Kanō's plan. He wanted judo to teach students to think clearly, act fairly and stay healthy. Teachers could fit it into a school day.

lessons.title: Ranks You Can See
lessons.mainIdea: In 1883, Kanō gave the first dan ranks, and later belts made those ranks easy to see.
reading: Old jujutsu schools gave scrolls and licenses to show a student's level. Kanō wanted a clearer ladder. In 1883, he gave the first *dan* rank to two students, Saigo Shiro and Tomita Tsunejiro. The first dan is called shodan.
Dan means step or level. Ranks below dan are called *kyu*. A student moves up through the kyu ranks first. Then the dan ranks begin at first dan and count upward.

Later, judo players with a dan rank wore a black belt. The belt made rank easy to see across a room. Other Japanese arts, and then arts in many countries, borrowed this idea of dan, kyu and colored belts.

words.d: a rank in judo and other arts meaning step or level; black-belt ranks are dan ranks

lessons.title: Two Big Ideas
lessons.mainIdea: Kanō summed up judo in two ideas: best use of energy, and mutual welfare and benefit.
reading: Kanō wrote about judo for many years. He boiled his ideas down into two short sayings in Japanese. In 1922, he started the Kodokan Culture Society to share them more widely.
The first saying is *seiryoku zen'yo*. It is often put in English as maximum efficiency, or the best use of energy. Kanō said this idea could guide study, work and daily life, not only judo.

The second saying is *jita kyoei*. It means mutual welfare and benefit, or you and others doing well together. Kanō hoped judo students would help their communities. Many judo schools still post these two sayings on the wall.

words.d: Kanō's saying about the best use of energy, often called maximum efficiency
Kanō's saying meaning mutual welfare and benefit, or doing well together

lessons.title: Kanō and the Olympics
lessons.mainIdea: Kanō became the first Asian member of the International Olympic Committee in 1909 and led Japan's first Olympic team in 1912.
reading: The *International Olympic Committee*, or IOC, runs the Olympic Games. In 1909, Jigorō Kanō joined it. He was the first member from Asia. He served on it for almost thirty years.

In 1912, Japan sent athletes to the Olympic Games for the first time. The Games were in Stockholm, Sweden. Japan sent two athletes, a runner in the marathon and a sprinter. Kanō led this small *delegation*.

Kanō worked to bring the Olympics to Tokyo. In 1936, the IOC chose Tokyo for the 1940 Games. Kanō died in 1938 on a ship on his way home from an IOC meeting in Cairo, Egypt. Because of war, the 1940 Tokyo Games never took place.

words.d: the group that runs the Olympic Games, called the IOC

lessons.title: Tokyo 1964
lessons.mainIdea: Judo became an Olympic sport at the 1964 Tokyo Games, the first Olympic Games held in Asia.
reading: In 1964, the Olympic Games finally came to Tokyo. They were the first Olympics held in Asia. Judo was on the program for the first time. It was the first Olympic sport that began in Japan.
Japan built a new hall for the judo contests. It is called the *Nippon Budokan*. It opened in 1964. Men competed in four groups: three *weight classes* and an open class for any size.

Japan won three of the four gold medals. The open class went to Anton Geesink of the Netherlands. He beat Kaminaga Akio of Japan in the final. His win showed that judo now belonged to the world, not only to Japan.

words.d: the hall in Tokyo built for judo at the 1964 Olympic Games

lessons.title: Women on the Mat
lessons.mainIdea: Women trained in judo early, but they waited until 1992 for Olympic judo medals.
reading: Kanō taught some women judo in private in its early years. In 1926, the Kodokan opened a *women's section*. It was a separate program for women and girls. Still, for many years women were kept out of most judo contests.

In the United States, Rena "Rusty" Kanokogi pushed for change. She organized the first Women's World Judo Championships. They took place in New York City in 1980. She also worked to get women's judo into the Olympics.

Women's judo was a demonstration event at the 1988 Seoul Olympics. A *demonstration* event shows a sport but gives no official medals. In 1992, at Barcelona, women competed for Olympic judo medals for the first time.

words.d: a separate program for women and girls; the Kodokan opened one in 1926

chapters.title: Why a Code Matters
chapters.bigQuestion: What changes when a fighting practice gets a written rulebook?

story.title: A Page Says Begin
story.kicker: Two players in white and blue jackets wait for one word from the referee.
paragraphs: A big hall hums with voices. Square mats cover the floor. At the edge of one mat stand two judo players. One wears a white jacket. The other wears a blue one.

Each player bows before stepping onto the mat. In judo, this bow is called rei. It is a sign of respect toward the other player. The rulebook says when it happens, so it is the same in Paris, Tokyo or Chicago.
A referee stands between them. The referee says one Japanese word: hajime. It means begin. Before that word, the match has not started. After it, the rules are in force.
Later the referee will say sore made. It means that is all. The players bow again and leave the mat. A scoreboard shows who won and why. The judges and the rules decide, not the crowd.
None of this is left to chance. A written code says where the match happens, how it starts, how it ends and who decides. That code lets strangers from different countries meet on the same mat.
story.think: Why might players from different countries need the same written rules?

lessons.title: Every School Its Own Way
lessons.mainIdea: Before judo had a shared contest code, each jujutsu school had its own customs, so matches between schools had no common rules.
reading: In old Japan, each jujutsu ryu had its own customs. One school might allow things another school forbade. There was no single book that every school agreed to follow.

When students from two schools met, they had to agree on terms first. Sometimes they could not agree. Without shared rules, it was hard to say who had won fairly. It was also hard to keep people from getting hurt.
Kanō wanted judo contests to be fair and safer. The Kodokan wrote down rules for *contests*, or official matches. By about 1900, it had a written set of contest rules with a *referee* in charge.

words.d: an official match between two players, run by rules
the official who runs a match and makes sure the rules are followed

check.why: A referee runs the match and makes sure the rules are followed.

check.q: About when did the Kodokan have written contest rules?

lessons.title: Prizefights in England
lessons.mainIdea: In England in the 1700s and 1800s, boxers fought bare-handed for prize money under rules that changed over time.
reading: Far from Japan, England had its own fighting world. In the 1700s, boxers fought for money in *prizefights*. They fought with bare hands, so this is called *bare-knuckle* boxing. Many prizefights were against the law, but crowds still came.

In 1743, a London boxer named Jack Broughton wrote a short set of rules for his boxing hall. They are among the first written boxing rules. In 1838, a longer set called the London Prize Ring Rules came out.
Under these older rules, a round ended when a boxer went down. A fight could go on for many rounds and last for hours. Serious injuries were common. People began to ask for safer rules.

words.d: a boxing match fought for money
boxing with bare hands and no gloves
rules for bare-knuckle boxing first published in England in 1838

lessons.title: A Page with Twelve Rules
lessons.mainIdea: The Queensberry Rules of 1867 were written by John Graham Chambers and named for the Marquess of Queensberry who backed them.
reading: In 1867, a new set of boxing rules was published in England. It had twelve short rules. A sportsman named John Graham Chambers wrote them. They carry the name of John Sholto Douglas, the ninth *Marquess* of Queensberry, who supported them.
So the rules are named for their backer, not their writer. That happens often in history. A famous name can help a new idea spread. People still call them the *Queensberry Rules*.
The rules asked boxers to wear *gloves* of good quality. They set the ring at 24 feet across. They called for a fair stand-up boxing match. These rules shaped modern boxing.

words.d: a title for a British noble; the Marquess of Queensberry lent his name to the 1867 rules
twelve boxing rules published in England in 1867 that called for gloves and timed rounds

lessons.title: Rounds and a Count
lessons.mainIdea: The Queensberry Rules set timed rounds, a rest between them and a ten-second count after a fall.
reading: The old prize ring had no clock for rounds. The Queensberry Rules changed that. Each *round* lasted three minutes. Then the boxers rested for one minute.
The rules also added a *count*. If a boxer went down, he had ten seconds to get up on his own. If he could not, the other boxer won. This gave every match a clear end.
A clock made boxing easier to judge. It also made matches shorter and more alike from place to place. Many other sports later used timed rounds or periods in the same way.

words.d: one timed part of a boxing match
the ten seconds a boxer who is down has to get up under the Queensberry Rules

check.why: Timed rounds made matches shorter, more alike and easier to judge.

lessons.title: Gloves Win the Title
lessons.mainIdea: In 1892, the heavyweight title changed hands in a gloved fight, and amateur boxing grew under the new rules.
reading: For years, bare-knuckle and gloved boxing went on side by side. John L. Sullivan was the last bare-knuckle heavyweight champion. In 1892, in New Orleans, he lost the title to James J. Corbett. They fought with gloves under Queensberry rules.
Clubs for *amateurs* also grew. An amateur takes part for sport, not for money. In 1880, the Amateur Boxing Association was founded in England. It held yearly championships.
Boxing joined the Olympics in 1904 at St. Louis. Women waited much longer. Women's boxing first became an Olympic event in 2012 in London. That was 108 years after men's boxing began at the Games.

words.d: a person who takes part in a sport for its own sake, not for money
the class for the heaviest boxers

lessons.title: A Start and an End
lessons.mainIdea: Judo rules give every match a clear start and end, with a bow and set words from the referee.
reading: Judo contests follow a set order. Players bow at the edge of the mat and again facing each other. This bow is called *rei*. In judo schools, it is described as a sign of respect for the other player.
The referee starts the match with the word *hajime*, meaning begin. The word matte means wait, and it pauses the match. The words sore made mean that is all, and they end it.

These words are Japanese, and they stayed Japanese as judo spread. A referee in Brazil, France or the United States uses the same words. Shared words help players who speak different languages understand the match.

words.d: the bow in judo, described in judo schools as a sign of respect
the Japanese word a judo referee uses to begin a match; it means begin

lessons.title: Matched by Weight
lessons.mainIdea: Weight classes group players of similar size, a rule that grew from four Olympic judo groups in 1964 to seven for men and seven for women.
reading: Early judo had no weight classes. Kanō taught that skill could beat size. Big and small players met in the same contests. The All-Japan Judo Championships, first held in 1930, still have no weight classes.

Many people thought size made contests unfair. At the 1964 Olympics, judo used three weight classes plus an open class. Over time, more classes were added. Today Olympic judo has seven *divisions* for men and seven for women.
Boxing and wrestling also use weight classes. The idea is the same in each sport. A *weigh-in* before the contest checks that each player is in the right group.

lessons.title: One Blue, One White
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1990s, the world judo federation approved a blue jacket so judges and fans could tell the two players apart.
reading: For most of judo's history, both players wore white. A judo uniform is called a *judogi*. It has a heavy cotton jacket, pants and a belt. White judogi stayed the custom at the Kodokan.

When two players in white move fast, it can be hard to tell them apart. In the 1990s, the world judo federation approved a *blue judogi*. In top contests, one player now wears blue and one wears white.

Not everyone liked the change. Some in Japan wanted to keep white as a tradition. Supporters said blue helped judges, fans and television viewers. The debate shows that rules can carry feelings as well as facts.

words.d: the judo uniform: a heavy cotton jacket, pants and a belt

lessons.title: Bodies That Keep the Rules
lessons.mainIdea: International federations write and update the rules for their sports so contests match from country to country.
reading: A *federation* is a group of national bodies that agree to share one set of rules. The International Judo Federation, or IJF, was founded in 1951. It writes the rules for world judo contests. It held the first World Judo Championships in Tokyo in 1956.
Other arts have their own federations. The International Fencing Federation was founded in Paris in 1913. World Taekwondo was founded in 1973. Each one keeps a *rulebook* and updates it.
Federations also decide who may enter, how referees are trained and how records are kept. The Olympics works with these federations. Without one, a sport cannot easily join the Games.

words.d: a group of national bodies that agree to share one set of rules
a written set of rules that everyone in a sport agrees to follow

lessons.title: Judo After 1945
lessons.mainIdea: After World War II, martial arts were stopped in Japanese schools for several years, then judo returned as a sport.
reading: Japan lost World War II in 1945. The Allied forces, led by the United States, then *occupied* Japan until 1952. The occupation leaders worried that martial arts had been used to train young people for war.
For several years, martial arts training was stopped in Japanese schools. Judo leaders argued that judo was a sport and a form of education. Around 1950, judo came back into schools.
Judo's written rules helped make that case. A sport with a rulebook, a referee and weight rules looked like school sport, not war training. Within twenty years, Tokyo hosted Olympic judo.

words.d: when another country's forces take control of a place for a time

lessons.title: Judo Clubs in America
lessons.mainIdea: Japanese immigrants brought judo to the United States, and their clubs kept going even during the World War II camps.
reading: Judo reached the United States in the early 1900s. In 1904, a Kodokan teacher named Yamashita Yoshitsugu taught judo to President Theodore Roosevelt at the White House. Japanese immigrants also opened judo clubs in cities like Seattle, San Francisco and Los Angeles.

In 1942, President Franklin Roosevelt signed *Executive Order 9066*. It led the government to force about 120,000 Japanese Americans from the West Coast into camps. Most were American citizens. Judo clubs were started inside several camps, such as Manzanar in California.
After the war, judo grew across the country. Many judo clubs in America today trace their start to Japanese American teachers. In 1988, the United States government formally apologized for the camps.

words.d: the 1942 order that led to forcing Japanese Americans into camps
